channel.title: Keith Dunstan
channel.description: The collected literary works of Keith Dunstan OAM

item.title: Royalty
item.description: A survey of two centuries of Australian royal-knocking, from the colonial press's attacks on Prince Alfred's brothel visits and the Bulletin's sustained assault on the Guelph family through the sedition trial of the labor journal Tocsin, the abdication crisis of Edward VIII, and the 1967 prosecution of the satirical journal Tom Thumb for a mock interview with Prince Philip.

item.title: Australian Myths
item.description: Examines the knocking of Australia's most sacred national myths, from the vicious attacks on Ned Kelly in Melbourne Punch and the homosexuality allegation that proved the one knock too far, through the sustained persecution of Les Darcy as a wartime shirker, the failed attempts to deflate Don Bradman and Kingsford Smith, and the long campaign against the Sydney Harbour Bridge and the Melbourne Shrine of Remembrance, ending with the Anzac Day controversies of the 1960s.

item.title: Australian Writers
item.description: Traces the long contempt shown to Australian writers, from the colonial press's dismissal of Adam Lindsay Gordon and the Victorian Parliament's refusal to grant a pension to Marcus Clarke's destitute widow, through Henry Lawson's fury at being ignored, the decades of neglect suffered by Joseph Furphy and Henry Handel Richardson, D. H. Lawrence's savage reception, the Ern Malley hoax and the prosecution of Max Harris, the critical savaging of Patrick White, and the knocking of Germaine Greer and Barry Humphries on their return from overseas triumph.

item.title: Australian Artists
item.description: Traces the knocking of Australian visual artists from the 1889 Impressionist Exhibition — savaged by critic James Smith — through the Lindsay obscenity battles, the Dobell Archibald Prize court case, the controversy over Drysdale's Melrose Prize winner, and Sidney Nolan and Charles Blackman's rough receptions, to a closing note that artists are finally, by 1971, almost as respectable as sportsmen.

item.title: The Australian Stage
item.description: Traces the knocking of the Australian stage from Lola Montez's 1855 Spider Dance controversy and Harry Seekamp's Ballarat horsewhipping through The Triad's savage music and theatre criticism, Nellie Melba's battles with John Norton, Frank Thring's career as a drama critic, the hostile reception given to Australian plays including Summer of the Seventeenth Doll and The One Day of the Year, the Katherine Brisbane libel case, and David Williamson's The Removalists, ending with a collection of ABC-era music criticism.

item.title: The Monash Story: Keeping Them Down on the Farm
item.description: A portrait of Monash University three years after its unexpectedly early opening, examining its car-dependent Clayton campus, its race to become the world's fastest-growing university, its chronic underfunding, and the outsized personalities shaping its character.

item.title: O, the Opulence of O!
item.description: A behind-the-scenes tour of Reg Ansett's Austarama TV studio at Nunawading, showcasing the opulent new Channel O before its August 1964 launch, with a pointed reminder of Ansett's 1963 promise to show Australians what Australia has to offer.

item.title: Now Watch Out for Those Inside Stories!
item.description: Keith Dunstan enrols at the Australian Academy of Investigation, a Collins Street school for private detectives run by a former Melbourne CIB man, and is disillusioned to find the work is mostly insurance claims and divorce surveillance, not espionage.

item.title: A Noble £10m Home for a Noble Game
item.description: The Victorian Football League unveils plans for a vast new stadium at Waverley, to hold 157,000 spectators and cost £14 million for its first stage, prompting Keith Dunstan to weigh the ambition against the practical difficulties of financing it and luring crowds 15 miles from the city.

item.title: For Tourists: Pies, Hares, and Cast-Iron
item.description: A satirical tourism plan for Melbourne, proposing pie-factory visits, live hare coursing, Percy Cerutty runs up the Portsea sandhills, and the restoration of Little Lonsdale Street's seedy glamour to pull American visitors away from the sinful East.

item.title: A Century Could Be Just Around the Bend
item.description: A sharp critique of the Victorian Railways' chronic derailment problem and its causes, tracing the system's 'muddled economy' back to a 1949 British transport expert's report that found the VR strangled by political interference, fantastically cheap freight rates, and a shortage of staff that any private employer could have solved by paying above award.

item.title: The Moss Spreads in Spring Street
item.description: A history of Victoria's ferocious Liberal-Country Party rivalry, from the 1921 fall of the Lawson government to the 1964 supply crisis in which Country Party leader Moss forced a complete surrender from Premier Bolte.

item.title: Oh, Bondi! Oh, Surfers! Oh, OH, St. Kilda!
item.description: The campaign by Melbourne's Victorian Federation of Catholic Mothers to ban bikinis from bayside beaches prompts a survey of the unlikely coalition of voices for and against, from Ron Barassi's wife to Premier Bolte and the bikini manufacturer who announced he would double production.

item.title: A Feasibility Study of a Hot Potato
item.description: Melbourne's push to host a World Fair in the early 1970s, led by Lord Mayor Leo Curtis and former Lord Mayor Sir Maurice Nathan, who lobbied Prime Minister Sir Robert Menzies and sought £50,000 from local backers to fund a feasibility study, with Essendon Airport floated as the ideal site once civil aviation vacated it for Tullamarine.

item.title: The Hot Dog is Still Too Thin / Radio Australia: The World's Most Successful
item.description: On the eve of Radio Australia's 25th birthday, a visit to its cramped Melbourne headquarters reveals the world's most-listened-to overseas radio service, ahead of the BBC and Voice of America, sustained by a quarter-million letters a year from listeners across Asia.

item.title: Like When King Edward Abdicated
item.description: Norm Smith's sacking and sudden reinstatement as Melbourne's football coach send the city into mourning, saturate the newspapers and television, and expose the club's patrician habits.

item.title: Eyestrain for Art's Sake
item.description: Keith Dunstan surveys the 13th Melbourne International Film Festival at the Palais Theatre in St Kilda, celebrating its world-class program while lamenting the bureaucratic obstacles of censorship and customs restrictions that hamper what is one of the world's finest film festivals.

item.title: Penguins, Pies, and Megapodes
item.description: The Mallee Fowl, a remarkable megapode bird facing extinction, gets a new 15,000-acre wildlife reserve near Mildura following advocacy by the Victorian Fisheries and Wildlife Department, with the Penguin Parade at Phillip Island and lyrebirds at Sherbrooke Forest rounding out Victoria's bird attractions for the growing flood of American birdwatching tourists.

item.title: Dialling for a Prayer and a Bet
item.description: Victoria's Totalisator Agency Board has quietly become a £40-million-a-year institution, bringing off-course betting into sterile shopfronts next to pubs and banks while channelling millions to hospitals, charities and racing clubs, as New South Wales and South Australia move to adopt the same system.

item.title: No Sunday Tumbling or Burletta Yet
item.description: A survey of Melbourne's Sunday laws, tracing the Sabbatarian battles of the 1880s through to Chief Secretary Arthur Rylah's cautious 1964 suggestion that theatres might open on Sundays, and the near-total public silence that greeted it.

item.title: Queuing for the Final Cachet
item.description: A portrait of Melbourne's devotion to queuing for VFL finals tickets, following two Essendon supporters who camped outside the MCG for days through snow and wind and ultimately charmed the Melbourne Cricket Club secretary over toast cooked on a primus stove.

item.title: Night of High Drama
item.description: The annual race between Melbourne television stations GTV-9 and HSV-7 to be first on air with the Brownlow Medal winner, a battle won five years running by HSV's Mike Williamson through a combination of pre-taped interviews, hidden surveillance and a terrifying drive through Elsternwick Junction.

item.title: The Rag Trade: 'A Goddamn Crazy Business...'
item.description: A four-page portrait of Melbourne's garment industry centred on Flinders Lane, tracing its history from the great warehouses of the pre-war era through the rise of specialist manufacturers, the menace of design pirates, the problem of bad debts, and the perpetual uncertainty of guessing what women will wear two years hence.

item.title: The Week of the Great White Fleet
item.description: A comparison of the 1964 American warship visit to Melbourne with the legendary 1908 arrival of the Great White Fleet, when 16 battleships under Admiral Sperry drew half a million people to the city in a single day and the party for naval ratings at the Exhibition Building outshone every other entertainment of the tour.

item.title: High Jinks in the Hard Top
item.description: A tour of Melbourne's ambitious new entertainment projects, including the Palladium Entertainment Centre with its twin theatres and Maxim's restaurant, and a rival rooftop licensed restaurant opening on Melbourne Cup eve at the National Mutual Centre.

item.title: Mr Borg's Auction in SE2
item.description: A vivid account of the Toorak household auction of Raymond Borg's house in Yarradale Road, where the crowd's main fascination was watching used-car dealer Emmanuel Margolin quietly buy back the Ming bronzes, Sevres vases and stuffed eagle he had been forced to sell at an earlier auction during the credit squeeze.

item.title: What's Been Missin' from Kissin'
item.description: A report on the Cutex flavoured-lipstick launch party in Melbourne, where Cherry Kiss, Peppermint Kiss and Caramel Kiss were unveiled to an audience including Footscray captain-coach Ted Whitten, with the assembled press left to judge whether taste and fragrance really did add a new dimension to cosmetics.

item.title: Point Cook: More Choosy Than Ever
item.description: A profile of the RAAF's officer training academy at Point Cook, tracing the base's history from Sir Richard Williams's first flight in 1914 to the newly degree-granting RAAF Academy of 1964, where cadets study physics alongside their flying.

item.title: The Explosive Vino di Carlton and Fitzroy
item.description: A survey of Melbourne's home wine-making boom, centred on Carlton and Fitzroy, where tens of thousands of Italian and Greek families were producing a million gallons a year in backyard stills and laundry sinks.

item.title: You Need More Than a 'D' in Toorak
item.description: The opening of 'Nareeb', Toorak's last great private estate, for public auction draws 15,000 visitors to the 53-acre Kooyong Road property unchanged since 1888, where the contents, from a 1920 Rolls-Royce to aspidistras, sell for over £18,000.
